## Sine and Cosine Series

- **Starting point:** Stone-Weierstrass (Ch 12) tells us trigonometric polynomials are dense in $C(\mathbb{T})$, hence in $L^2$
- We know SOME trig polynomial gets arbitrarily close to $f$; we want the BEST one
- **Orthogonality of sines:** direct computation shows $\int_0^\pi \sin(mx)\sin(nx)\, dx = \frac{\pi}{2}\delta_{mn}$
- **Best $L^2$ approximation:** among all $\sum_{n=1}^N a_n \sin(nx)$, which minimizes $\|f - \sum a_n \sin(nx)\|_2^2$?
- Orthogonality implies: best approximation is orthogonal projection
- **Formula forced:** $b_n = \frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(nx)\, dx$
- **Bessel's inequality:** $\sum_{n=1}^\infty |b_n|^2 \leq \frac{2}{\pi}\|f\|_2^2$
- **Proof:** expand $\|f - S_N\|^2 \geq 0$, rearrange
- **$L^2$ convergence:** density says some trig polynomials converge to $f$; Fourier partial sums are the BEST trig polynomials of each degree; so Fourier partial sums converge
- **Parseval's identity:** $\sum_{n=1}^\infty |b_n|^2 = \frac{2}{\pi}\|f\|_2^2$ (Bessel becomes equality)
- **The full circle:** on $[-\pi, \pi]$ periodic, need $\{1, \cos(nx), \sin(nx)\}$
- Same theory applies; guided exercises develop this case
